# Background

## Embodied Cognition Approach
- Readers rely on both linguistic and non-linguistic information during language processing (e.g., Barsalou, 2008).

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
#| out.width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("fig/embodiment.png")
```

## Terai (2023, *Doctoral thesis*)

- Activation of Object color information (e.g., *bear* = BROWN)

- Semantic Stroop task
  1. Read a sentence (e.g., *Joe was excited to see a bear in the woods.*)
  2. A keyword is presented in color ( <font color="brown">**bear**</font> )
  3. Answer the color of the font

## Stroop Effect
### Receiving inconsistent information causes inhibition.

<center>
<span style="font-size: 700%; color: blue;">Red </span>
<span style="font-size: 700%; color: red;"> Blue</span>
</center>
<center>
<span style="font-size: 700%; color: red;">Red </span>

</center>

## Stroop Effect

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
#| out.width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("fig/stroop.png")
```

- The presence of the Stroop effect is evidence of color activation

## Terai (2023, *Doctoral thesis*)

- Two types of sentences

  - e.g., *Joe was excited to see a bear in the woods*: **brown bear**

  - e.g., *Joe was excited to see a bear at the North Pole*: **polar bear**

- Three font colors

  - typical color: *bear* in Brown
  
  - atypical color: *bear* in White

  - unrelated color: *bear* in Green

## Terai (2023, *Doctoral thesis*)
- First language: English speakers, Japanese speakers.
- Reaction times were faster when the indicated color matched the font color, compared to when they mismatched.
- Readers activated only the typical color of an object.
  
    - *Joe was excited to see a bear in the woods*: 🐻

    - *Joe was excited to see a bear at the North Pole*: 🐻

- There was no evidence of atypical color activation.

::: {.callout-note}
L1 English: [Terai & Yamashita (in Print, *Journal of Psycholinguistic Research*)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10936-026-10310-4)
:::

## Terai (2023, *Doctoral thesis*)

- Japanese speakers performed in English

    - Interaction of second language proficiency and typicality 

- Higher proficiency learners showed larger Stroop effects

## Terai (2026, *Applied Psycholinguistics*)

- Participants completed the semantic Stroop task in both Japanese and English

    - Language was a within-subject design

- They also completed a lexical decision task to measure their response times to the words used in the Stroop task

## Summary of the Previous Studies

- Color information is not always activated (Weak Embodiment)

    - Presence of Context may elicit stronger Stroop effect?

- A certain level of L2 proficiency may be necessary for L2 processing


## Toward the Study

- Did presence of context elicite larger Stroop effects than without presenting sentences?

  - Experiment Type (Sentence- / Without-Sentence) was within-subject factor

# The Study

## Research Hypotheses

1. The Stroop effect will be smaller in the word-only Stroop task.

2. The Stroop effect will be larger for learners with higher L2 proficiency.

## Participants
- 24 Japanese learners of English were recruited at a Japanese university. 

- English proficiency: Scores of a yes-no vocabulary size test (Meara & Miralpeix, 2015). 

  - Relatively low-level English proficiency (*M* = 2223, Range = 250--4913)

![](fig/yesnotest.png)

## Procedures

- Experiment Type and Language of the task was also withn-subject design.

    - e.g., Participant A: with-sentence (ENG), word-only (JPN)

    - e.g., Participant B: with-sentence (JPN), word-only (ENG)

## Difference of the Task (1)
- The Stroop word was inserted in black font before Stroop phase

    - By adding this phase, the present study made the two tasks more comparable: the critical difference between the tasks was whether the prior presentation consisted of a sentence or a single word.

![](fig/thisstudy.png)

- Independent variables:

    - Task type (sentence-context vs. word-only)
    
    - Task language (L1 vs. L2)

## Hypothesis 1
::: {style="background-color: #cde5f5; border: 1px solid steelblue; padding: 10px; border-radius: 6px;"}
✖ The Stroop effect will be smaller in the word-only Stroop task.
:::

- There was no large difference of Stroop effect of sentence- and word-only Stroop task

  - Presenting sentences does not necessarily facilitate color activation

  - Typical color information may be activated even in word-level.
  
- Prior presentation of words may have facilitate semantic processing compared with a task without such a presentation phase. 
 
## Hypothesis 2
![](fig/FigB.png)


## Hypothesis 2

::: {style="background-color: #cde5f5; border: 1px solid steelblue; padding: 10px; border-radius: 6px;"}
⭕ The Stroop effect will be larger for learners with higher L2 proficiency.
::: 

- Learners with higher proficiency tended to show a larger Stroop effect than learners with lower proficiency in L2 tasks, regardless of task type.

  - Consistent with Terai (2023)

## Conclusion
- Readers are likely to activate typical color of the inferred object without reading color words (e.g., red, blue, green).

- In L2 processing, only higher L2 proficiency learners show activation of colors.
